## Custom model design

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/index/03-concept; notes-page: custom-models/index.qmd; note-sha256: 2c697392dde3dddaad91cd9968b5757ff4f2291c09e4d55a3e800970e81e2a39; role: concept -->

A custom likelihood should encode those parts without turning a response into direct access to the target property.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An annotation is an observed response produced by a measurement procedure. It is not the linguistic property that the procedure is meant to inform. The measurement procedure connects a linguistic unit, a prompt, an annotator, a response scale, and the recorded answer. A custom likelihood should encode those parts without turning a response into direct access to the target property.

[Sources]

https://aclanthology.org/2020.lrec-1.699/
https://aclanthology.org/2022.tacl-1.2/
https://pypi.org/project/decomp/0.3.2/

https://turkishpropbank.github.io/
:::

## Custom model design

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/index/04-concept; notes-page: custom-models/index.qmd; note-sha256: 2c697392dde3dddaad91cd9968b5757ff4f2291c09e4d55a3e800970e81e2a39; role: concept -->

The natural-parts task in Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS) records binary answers about predicate nodes in English dependency graphs; Gantt, Glass, and White (2022) describe the event-structure protocol.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This module uses two annotation resources, one of them non-English. The natural-parts task in Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS) records binary answers about predicate nodes in English dependency graphs; Gantt, Glass, and White (2022) describe the event-structure protocol. The course extract is pinned to the official `decomp` 0.3.2 release: the data are CC BY-SA 4.0, while the toolkit code is MIT-licensed. The ITU/IMST Turkish PropBank records worker selections among predicate-specific role descriptions, followed by aggregation and adjudication; the project release supplies the source data and guidelines.

[Sources]

https://aclanthology.org/2022.tacl-1.2/
https://pypi.org/project/decomp/0.3.2/
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-017-9390-y
https://turkishpropbank.github.io/
:::

## From the protocol to a probability model

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/index/07-concept; notes-page: custom-models/index.qmd; note-sha256: 2c697392dde3dddaad91cd9968b5757ff4f2291c09e4d55a3e800970e81e2a39; role: concept -->

Parameter recovery asks whether the complete procedure can recover known values under the released incidence design.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A data-generating process first specifies the random steps that could produce the UDS gate responses. Writing a joint model then translates those steps into a joint probability distribution over the observed item--annotator pairs. Parameter recovery asks whether the complete procedure can recover known values under the released incidence design.

Keeping those units distinct fixes the product terms in the likelihood and the populations represented by the random effects.

## Data-generating processes

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/generative-stories/02-concept; notes-page: custom-models/generative-stories.qmd; note-sha256: 18a9f4fcae1fbdf2ddf4ee7d1c319c3f029b4d722a326813245683cfc8b18e59; role: concept -->

Gantt, Glass, and White (2022) describe the event protocol and its conditional branches, while the Decomp documentation describes the released semantic graph attributes.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The event-structure annotations in Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS) attach properties to predicate nodes anchored in sentence context. In the natural-parts task, an annotator first reports whether the situation described by a predicate has natural subparts. The response is evidence about event structure under this instrument; it is not event structure itself. Gantt, Glass, and White (2022) describe the event protocol and its conditional branches, while the Decomp documentation describes the released semantic graph attributes.

## Stating one step at a time (1 of 2) {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/generative-stories/07-list; notes-page: custom-models/generative-stories.qmd; note-sha256: 18a9f4fcae1fbdf2ddf4ee7d1c319c3f029b4d722a326813245683cfc8b18e59; role: list -->

Let $i$ index predicate nodes and $j$ index annotators. A first DGP has four steps.

1. Draw an item deviation $u_i$ from an item population.
2. Draw an annotator deviation $a_j$ from an annotator population.
3. Map the population location and deviations to a yes probability $\pi_{ij}$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $i$ index predicate nodes and $j$ index annotators. A first DGP has four steps. Draw an item deviation $u_i$ from an item population. Draw an annotator deviation $a_j$ from an annotator population. Map the population location and deviations to a yes probability $\pi_{ij}$.

## Stating one step at a time {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/generative-stories/09-math; notes-page: custom-models/generative-stories.qmd; note-sha256: 18a9f4fcae1fbdf2ddf4ee7d1c319c3f029b4d722a326813245683cfc8b18e59; role: math -->

The corresponding model is

$$
u_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\text{item}}^2),
\qquad
a_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\text{annotator}}^2),
$$

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})=\alpha+u_i+a_j,
\qquad
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The corresponding model is

a_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\text{annotator}}^2),

\qquad
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}).

## Declaring what is outside the process

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/generative-stories/14-concept; notes-page: custom-models/generative-stories.qmd; note-sha256: 18a9f4fcae1fbdf2ddf4ee7d1c319c3f029b4d722a326813245683cfc8b18e59; role: concept -->

The released normalized confidence field is thus not treated as an additional raw judgment.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The original protocol uses the natural-parts answer to determine which later questions appear. A yes reveals questions about part similarity and part duration; a no reveals questions about whole-event duration and dynamicity. This display logic matters, but the present extract does not contain audited raw responses to those branches. Raw confidence is also blocked: the paper describes a one-to-five scale, the package metadata describes a zero-to-four scale, and the inspected raw serialization repeats a duration response in the confidence position. The released normalized confidence field is thus not treated as an additional raw judgment.

[Sources]

https://aclanthology.org/2020.lrec-1.699/
https://aclanthology.org/2022.tacl-1.2/
https://decomp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/data/semantic-types.html
:::

## Declaring what is outside the process (1 of 2) {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/generative-stories/15-list; notes-page: custom-models/generative-stories.qmd; note-sha256: 18a9f4fcae1fbdf2ddf4ee7d1c319c3f029b4d722a326813245683cfc8b18e59; role: list -->

The narrower claim keeps every recorded variable in the likelihood and every omitted variable outside it.

1. Which quantity in the model is recorded directly?
2. Why do the rows for one item share $u_i$ but not $a_j$?
3. Why is an item identifier not a verb-lemma identifier?

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus this DGP is deliberately a model of the observed natural-parts gate. It is not a model of the complete event-structure instrument. The narrower claim keeps every recorded variable in the likelihood and every omitted variable outside it. Which quantity in the model is recorded directly? Why do the rows for one item share $u_i$ but not $a_j$? Why is an item identifier not a verb-lemma identifier?

## Declaring what is outside the process (2 of 2) {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/generative-stories/16-list; notes-page: custom-models/generative-stories.qmd; note-sha256: 18a9f4fcae1fbdf2ddf4ee7d1c319c3f029b4d722a326813245683cfc8b18e59; role: list -->

The narrower claim keeps every recorded variable in the likelihood and every omitted variable outside it.

4. Which response branches remain outside this model?

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus this DGP is deliberately a model of the observed natural-parts gate. It is not a model of the complete event-structure instrument. The narrower claim keeps every recorded variable in the likelihood and every omitted variable outside it. Which response branches remain outside this model?

## Writing a joint model

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/writing-a-joint-model/03-concept; notes-page: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd; note-sha256: 230e2e9f01303a7ed73a6ee00794ec0daf462f5d6abaa6847f3d9bf8b71401ca; role: concept -->

The product states which quantities are conditionally independent and which observations share an unobserved item value.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **joint probability model** assigns one factor to every random step in a data-generating process. This is the product rule applied to the annotation process. The product states which quantities are conditionally independent and which observations share an unobserved item value.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd
:::

## Loading the observed-pair set

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/writing-a-joint-model/04-concept; notes-page: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd; note-sha256: 230e2e9f01303a7ed73a6ee00794ec0daf462f5d6abaa6847f3d9bf8b71401ca; role: concept -->

It does not add factors for item-annotator combinations that were never observed.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $\mathcal O$ be the 2,955 item-annotator pairs stored in `observed_pairs`. The likelihood has one response factor for each row in this set. It does not add factors for item-annotator combinations that were never observed.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd
:::

## Translating steps into factors {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/writing-a-joint-model/05-math; notes-page: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd; note-sha256: 230e2e9f01303a7ed73a6ee00794ec0daf462f5d6abaa6847f3d9bf8b71401ca; role: math -->

Let $\theta_i$ be the log odds of a yes response for predicate-node item $i$ in the item-only model. Then

$$
\pi_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\theta_i),
\qquad
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
$$

and the item values follow

$$
\theta_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta^2).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $\theta_i$ be the log odds of a yes response for predicate-node item $i$ in the item-only model. Then

$$
\pi_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\theta_i),
\qquad
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
$$

and the item values follow

$$
\theta_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta^2).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd
:::

## Translating steps into factors {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/writing-a-joint-model/06-math; notes-page: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd; note-sha256: 230e2e9f01303a7ed73a6ee00794ec0daf462f5d6abaa6847f3d9bf8b71401ca; role: math -->

For observed responses $\mathbf y$ and item values $\boldsymbol\theta$, the joint distribution is

$$
f(\mathbf y,\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta)
=
\prod_i f(\theta_i\mid\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta)
\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathcal O}p(y_{ij}\mid\theta_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For observed responses $\mathbf y$ and item values $\boldsymbol\theta$, the joint distribution is

$$
f(\mathbf y,\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta)
=
\prod_i f(\theta_i\mid\mu_\theta,\tau_\theta)
\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathcal O}p(y_{ij}\mid\theta_i).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd
:::

## Translating steps into factors

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/writing-a-joint-model/07-concept; notes-page: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd; note-sha256: 230e2e9f01303a7ed73a6ee00794ec0daf462f5d6abaa6847f3d9bf8b71401ca; role: concept -->

Repeated occurrences of $\theta_i$ record the fact that responses to one predicate node share information.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The first product generates one item value per predicate node. The second generates each recorded response conditional on the item value named by that row. Repeated occurrences of $\theta_i$ record the fact that responses to one predicate node share information.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd
:::

## Translating steps into factors

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/writing-a-joint-model/08-concept; notes-page: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd; note-sha256: 230e2e9f01303a7ed73a6ee00794ec0daf462f5d6abaa6847f3d9bf8b71401ca; role: concept -->

Multiplication is commutative; the conditional arguments carry the dependency claim.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The order of multiplication does not describe temporal order. Multiplication is commutative; the conditional arguments carry the dependency claim.

## Separating observations from summaries {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/writing-a-joint-model/13-math; notes-page: custom-models/writing-a-joint-model.qmd; note-sha256: 230e2e9f01303a7ed73a6ee00794ec0daf462f5d6abaa6847f3d9bf8b71401ca; role: math -->

$$
\bar Y_i=\frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal O}Y_{ij}

is determined by response rows already in the likelihood.

## Evaluating parameter recovery {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/parameter-recovery/08-math; notes-page: custom-models/parameter-recovery.qmd; note-sha256: 96532fd16f46a51ca96dff9a2e9b9d8523c8c7aa4ce6bcb5eee3372f8278d99d; role: math -->

For replicate $s$, an error is $\widehat\theta_s-\theta_s$. Across $S$ replicates, estimated bias and root mean squared error are

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Bias}}
=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S(\widehat\theta_s-\theta_s),
$$

$$
\operatorname{RMSE}
=\sqrt{\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S
(\widehat\theta_s-\theta_s)^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For replicate $s$, an error is $\widehat\theta_s-\theta_s$. Across $S$ replicates, estimated bias and root mean squared error are

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Bias}}
=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S(\widehat\theta_s-\theta_s),
$$

$$
\operatorname{RMSE}
=\sqrt{\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S
(\widehat\theta_s-\theta_s)^2}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/parameter-recovery.qmd

## Evaluating parameter recovery

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/parameter-recovery/09-concept; notes-page: custom-models/parameter-recovery.qmd; note-sha256: 96532fd16f46a51ca96dff9a2e9b9d8523c8c7aa4ce6bcb5eee3372f8278d99d; role: concept -->

Maximum key-parameter $\widehat R$ at most $1.05$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The audit used medians and recovery correlations because the target includes population scales and high-dimensional latent orderings. Its prespecified thresholds were: median absolute intercept error at most $.25$; median absolute relative errors at most $.15$ for the item scale and $.25$ for the annotator scale; median correlations at least $.60$ for item effects, $.90$ for annotator effects, and $.65$ for conditional item probabilities; maximum key-parameter $\widehat R$ at most $1.05$; and no divergent transitions.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/parameter-recovery.qmd
:::

## Annotations are measurements {.section-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/annotations-as-measurements/01-section; notes-page: custom-models/annotations-as-measurements.qmd; note-sha256: d5250c885b8d08de39037f41defb8e1ceaf6653b5cca1315d9b1f567d3e62d00; role: section -->

The official project release provides the frames, crowd layers, and final annotations. The course extract is privacy-sanitized from the pinned project repository; it removes platform identifiers, locations, timestamps, and free text.

## Keeping three agreement quantities distinct

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/annotations-as-measurements/08-concept; notes-page: custom-models/annotations-as-measurements.qmd; note-sha256: d5250c885b8d08de39037f41defb8e1ceaf6653b5cca1315d9b1f567d3e62d00; role: concept -->

The three quantities have different observational units and denominators.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The paper reports Cohen's $\kappa=.936$ for an expert versus trust-weighted aggregate answers on 2,000 deliberately unambiguous test questions. It reports Fleiss' $\kappa=.65$ across varying workers on roughly 18,000 ordinary multi-category questions. The response above is a third quantity: an individual worker's binary match with the later adjudicated description. The three quantities have different observational units and denominators.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-017-9390-y
https://turkishpropbank.github.io/
https://github.com/turkishpropbank/turkishpropbank.github.io/tree/5cd9c9918c8a7f4fd62802387e04d14b995ecb66
:::

The resulting probability is a property of this released task, not a worker-competence score and not a replication of either $\kappa$ statistic.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This lesson asks whether individual agreement with adjudication differs between predicate-specific core descriptions and general adjunct-like descriptions. ## Fitting a crossed measurement model {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/annotations-as-measurements/11-math; notes-page: custom-models/annotations-as-measurements.qmd; note-sha256: d5250c885b8d08de39037f41defb8e1ceaf6653b5cca1315d9b1f567d3e62d00; role: math -->

Let $u_i$ be an item intercept and $v_j$ a worker intercept. The model is

$$
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}),
$$

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})
=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{Adjunct}_i+u_i+v_j,
$$

$$
u_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\text{item}}^2),
\qquad
v_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\text{worker}}^2).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $u_i$ be an item intercept and $v_j$ a worker intercept. The model is

$$
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}),
$$

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})
=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{Adjunct}_i+u_i+v_j,
$$

$$
u_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\text{item}}^2),
\qquad
v_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\text{worker}}^2).
$$

[Sources]

## Adding one location term {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/annotator-effects/06-math; notes-page: custom-models/annotator-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 4ea322b7793e1c0de5c424bfcd30d1b0dbb5bb17594b4e9a72b0828c21415289; role: math -->

Let $u_i$ be item $i$'s deviation and $a_j$ annotator $j$'s location effect. The response model is

$$
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}),
$$

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})=\alpha+u_i+a_j.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $u_i$ be item $i$'s deviation and $a_j$ annotator $j$'s location effect. The response model is

$$
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}),
$$

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})=\alpha+u_i+a_j.
$$

## Adding one location term {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/annotator-effects/07-math; notes-page: custom-models/annotator-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 4ea322b7793e1c0de5c424bfcd30d1b0dbb5bb17594b4e9a72b0828c21415289; role: math -->

The fitted model constructs its deviations from centered standard-normal vectors:

$$
u_i=\sigma_{\text{item}}
\left(z_i^{\text{item}}-\bar z^{\text{item}}\right),
\qquad
z_i^{\text{item}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
$$

$$
a_j=\sigma_{\text{annotator}}
\left(z_j^{\text{annotator}}-\bar z^{\text{annotator}}\right),
\qquad
z_j^{\text{annotator}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The fitted model constructs its deviations from centered standard-normal vectors:

$$
u_i=\sigma_{\text{item}}
\left(z_i^{\text{item}}-\bar z^{\text{item}}\right),
\qquad
z_i^{\text{item}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
$$

$$
a_j=\sigma_{\text{annotator}}
\left(z_j^{\text{annotator}}-\bar z^{\text{annotator}}\right),
\qquad
z_j^{\text{annotator}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).

## Adding one location term

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/annotator-effects/08-concept; notes-page: custom-models/annotator-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 4ea322b7793e1c0de5c424bfcd30d1b0dbb5bb17594b4e9a72b0828c21415289; role: concept -->

The effect is shared across responses, so it is not trial noise.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A positive $a_j$ raises the log odds of a yes response for every item judged by annotator $j$; a negative value lowers them. The effect is shared across responses, so it is not trial noise.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/annotator-effects.qmd
:::

The decomposition is not identified without a reference. For any constant $c$,

$$
(\alpha+u_i+c)+(a_j-c)=\alpha+u_i+a_j.
$$

The response probabilities do not change. Centering the realized effects imposes

$$
\sum_i u_i=0,
\qquad

## Fixing the coordinate system

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/annotator-effects/11-concept; notes-page: custom-models/annotator-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 4ea322b7793e1c0de5c424bfcd30d1b0dbb5bb17594b4e9a72b0828c21415289; role: concept -->

Under the convention, $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha+u_i)$ is the item probability with the annotator effect fixed at zero.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This convention fixes the latent origin. It does not assert that an annotator with effect zero has no response behavior. Under the convention, $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha+u_i)$ is the item probability with the annotator effect fixed at zero.

## Location is not every annotator difference

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/annotator-effects/15-concept; notes-page: custom-models/annotator-effects.qmd; note-sha256: 4ea322b7793e1c0de5c424bfcd30d1b0dbb5bb17594b4e9a72b0828c21415289; role: concept -->

The current binary data and recovery study support this smaller term; they do not support adding discrimination or threshold parameters without a new design check.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Annotators may differ in response consistency, interpretation, or use of an ordered scale. A location effect cannot represent those patterns. It shifts every predicted log odds in the same direction. The current binary data and recovery study support this smaller term; they do not support adding discrimination or threshold parameters without a new design check.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/annotator-effects.qmd
:::

## Writing the complete model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/uds-measurement-model/05-math; notes-page: custom-models/uds-measurement-model.qmd; note-sha256: 7c43fb927f4f444581bad045fcbff65d7e80bce6d71e1dae4e1b01ff803395e6; role: math -->

For each observed pair $(i,j)\in\mathcal O$,

$$
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}),
$$

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})
=\alpha+u_i+a_j.
$$

::: {.notes}

For each observed pair $(i,j)\in\mathcal O$,

$$

$$

$$

## Writing the complete model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/uds-measurement-model/06-math; notes-page: custom-models/uds-measurement-model.qmd; note-sha256: 7c43fb927f4f444581bad045fcbff65d7e80bce6d71e1dae4e1b01ff803395e6; role: math -->

The fitted deviations are effects constructed by centering non-centered standard-normal vectors,

$$
u_i=\sigma_{\text{item}}
\left(z_i^{\text{item}}-\bar z^{\text{item}}\right),
\qquad
z_i^{\text{item}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
$$

$$
a_j=\sigma_{\text{annotator}}
\left(z_j^{\text{annotator}}-\bar z^{\text{annotator}}\right),
\qquad
z_j^{\text{annotator}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The fitted deviations are effects constructed by centering non-centered standard-normal vectors,

$$
u_i=\sigma_{\text{item}}
\left(z_i^{\text{item}}-\bar z^{\text{item}}\right),
\qquad
z_i^{\text{item}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
$$

$$
a_j=\sigma_{\text{annotator}}
\left(z_j^{\text{annotator}}-\bar z^{\text{annotator}}\right),
\qquad
z_j^{\text{annotator}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
$$

## Writing the complete model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/uds-measurement-model/07-math; notes-page: custom-models/uds-measurement-model.qmd; note-sha256: 7c43fb927f4f444581bad045fcbff65d7e80bce6d71e1dae4e1b01ff803395e6; role: math -->

The priors are

$$
\alpha\sim\mathcal N(0,2.5^2),
$$

$$
\sigma_{\text{item}}\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(2),
\qquad
\sigma_{\text{annotator}}\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(2).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The priors are

$$

$$

## Writing the complete model {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/uds-measurement-model/08-math; notes-page: custom-models/uds-measurement-model.qmd; note-sha256: 7c43fb927f4f444581bad045fcbff65d7e80bce6d71e1dae4e1b01ff803395e6; role: math -->

Thus $\alpha$ is the log odds for an item and annotator at their respective origins, and

$$
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha+u_i)
$$

is item $i$'s yes probability with the annotator effect fixed at zero.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Since the scale parameters are constrained positive in Stan, the normal statements for them induce half-normal priors. Centering fixes both realized effect sums at zero. Thus $\alpha$ is the log odds for an item and annotator at their respective origins, and

$$
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha+u_i)
$$

is item $i$'s yes probability with the annotator effect fixed at zero.

[Sources]

https://aclanthology.org/2022.tacl-1.2/
:::

## Gated annotations

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/02-concept; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: concept -->

It is not a low value on that branch and not a failed attempt to answer a displayed question.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The UDS event protocol uses the natural-parts response as a gate. A yes displays questions about part similarity and average part duration; a no displays questions about whole-situation duration and dynamicity. An undisplayed response is thus **structurally missing**. It is not a low value on that branch and not a failed attempt to answer a displayed question.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd
:::

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The local extract supports numerical analysis of the observed natural-parts gate only. ## Factoring the gate and follow-up response

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/05-concept; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: concept -->

Write $\pi_{ij}$ for the gate probability and $f_Y(y_{ij}\mid\phi_{ij})$ for the conditional follow-up probability or density.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $G_{ij}=1$ when annotator $j$ reports that predicate-node item $i$ has natural parts, and let $G_{ij}=0$ otherwise. Let $Y_{ij}$ denote a response on the yes branch, such as part similarity. Write $\pi_{ij}$ for the gate probability and $f_Y(y_{ij}\mid\phi_{ij})$ for the conditional follow-up probability or density.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd
:::

## Factoring the gate and follow-up response {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/06-math; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: math -->

The observed response contribution is

$$
f_{G,Y}(g_{ij},y_{ij}^{\mathrm{obs}})
=
\begin{cases}
\pi_{ij}f_Y(y_{ij}\mid\phi_{ij}), & g_{ij}=1,\\
1-\pi_{ij}, & g_{ij}=0.
\end{cases}
$$

When $g_{ij}=1$, the record contributes a gate factor and a follow-up factor.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The observed response contribution is

$$
f_{G,Y}(g_{ij},y_{ij}^{\mathrm{obs}})
=
\begin{cases}
\pi_{ij}f_Y(y_{ij}\mid\phi_{ij}), & g_{ij}=1,\\
1-\pi_{ij}, & g_{ij}=0.
\end{cases}
$$

When $g_{ij}=1$, the record contributes a gate factor and a follow-up factor.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd
:::

## Factoring the gate and follow-up response

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/07-concept; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: concept -->

The second case never evaluates a density at an unrecorded follow-up value.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

When $g_{ij}=0$, it contributes only the negative-gate probability. The second case never evaluates a density at an unrecorded follow-up value.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd
:::

## Factoring the gate and follow-up response {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/08-math; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: math -->

The same factorization can be written as

$$
f_{G,Y}(g_{ij},y_{ij}^{\mathrm{obs}})
=
\left[\pi_{ij}f_Y(y_{ij}\mid\phi_{ij})\right]^{g_{ij}}
(1-\pi_{ij})^{1-g_{ij}},
$$

where the follow-up term is meaningful only for records on which the branch is observed.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The same factorization can be written as

$$
f_{G,Y}(g_{ij},y_{ij}^{\mathrm{obs}})
=
\left[\pi_{ij}f_Y(y_{ij}\mid\phi_{ij})\right]^{g_{ij}}
(1-\pi_{ij})^{1-g_{ij}},
$$

where the follow-up term is meaningful only for records on which the branch is observed.

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/13-math; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: math -->

## The follow-up target is conditional

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/14-concept; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: concept -->

Replacing an undisplayed part-similarity response with zero would merge two events: rejecting the gate and passing the gate while selecting the scale's lowest response.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

It would not estimate an unconditional property over all predicate nodes unless the model defined what the follow-up means when an annotator rejects the premise that natural parts exist. Replacing an undisplayed part-similarity response with zero would merge two events: rejecting the gate and passing the gate while selecting the scale's lowest response.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd
:::

## The follow-up target is conditional

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/15-concept; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: concept -->

The present gate fit cannot identify it.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The gate and a future follow-up model might share item or annotator quantities. For instance, an item that often passes the gate might also tend to receive a particular conditional response. But such dependence requires raw branch-bearing records, enough passed gates, a reconciled response scale, and a new recovery study. The present gate fit cannot identify it.

[Sources]

Course note: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd
:::

## Separating protocol absence from stochastic missingness

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/16-concept; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: concept -->

Protocol absence differs from the missing intended measurements discussed in missingness mechanisms: here the instrument defines no follow-up response after the incompatible gate value.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A rectangular data table may store `NA` for an undisplayed follow-up. The joint model, not the storage symbol, determines what that `NA` means. Protocol absence differs from the missing intended measurements discussed in missingness mechanisms: here the instrument defines no follow-up response after the incompatible gate value.

<!-- generated-slide-id: custom-model-design/gated-annotations/19-concept; notes-page: custom-models/gated-annotations.qmd; note-sha256: a07a7e6657f06897e653d3b0bf3e394910dd644a53fdf50f38d1bc198a6a628d; role: concept -->

Keeping the second component symbolic preserves the logic of the instrument without inventing data.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]
